newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union predicts Chrysler deal, but strike looms.
newsitem.headline: Canada union predicts Chrysler deal, but strike looms.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers predicted Tuesday that it will conclude a labour agreement with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit, but may not be able to resolve all issues before the midnight strike deadline.

"Even if we cannot resolve this today, it's clear over the next few days we will have a settlement that sets a new standard for working people throughout the country," CAW president Buzz Hargrove told reporters.
He said he would not consider extending the strike deadline despite the time lost in resolving the critical outsourcing issue.
"We are not going to lift the deadline," Hargrove said.
The union halted talks Monday afternoon on all issues except outsourcing, to try to force a deal.
Company officials said they were also worried there might not be enough time to resolve the rest of the issues since negotiators lost five hours to the halt on Monday night.
"We're certainly concerned about the little time remaining," said Chrysler Canada spokesman Walt McCall. "We think it's attainable, but it's going to be tough."

Company and union officials said the key issues left to resolve involved the economic package. The CAW said it was concerned about the company's demands for user fees and co-payments to the health care plan, as well as wages.
"Today we turn our full attention the economic package," McCall told Reuters.

Ken Lewenza, CAW chairman of the Chrysler bargaining team, said he was not optimistic that all the issues could be resolved in time to inform employees at Chrysler's five Canada plants whether to take strike action.
Some labour analysts said that might cause confusion and result in workers jumping the gun and walking out ahead of the strike deadline.

"The problem for the union is more making sure that when they say they won't go out until the deadline, that they won't," said Charlotte Yates, professor of labour relations at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario.
Lewenza told reporters he was confident there would be no work stoppage before 11:59 P.M. EDT. But he said stumbling blocks over economic issues might result in a strike.
Late Monday, the CAW and Chrysler Canada reached a critical deal limiting Chrysler's ability to outsource work.

"It gives us input into where they are heading in the future," Hargrove said. "The (contractual) language will include an embargo on the sale or closure of a workplace or a major part of a workplace during the life of this agreement."
Hargrove said a tentative agreement between the United Auto Workers and Ford Motor Co. on Monday may have made it possible for Chrysler to move ahead on outsourcing.

"The fact that (UAW President) Stephen Yokich and (Ford Chairman) Alex Trotman announced a tentative agreement at around seven o'clock last evening was one of the factors that allowed Chrysler to move ahead on this issue," he said.
Outsourcing involves the sale of plants or transfer of work to contractors whose employees are not generally members of the auto unions.
The union is expected to use its agreement with Chrysler as the pattern that it will try to force on the Canadian subsidiaries of Ford and General Motors Corp.
